ety.text: From Middle English womman, from earlier wimman, wifman, from Old English wīfmann (“woman”, literally “female person”), a compound of wīf (“woman, female”, whence English wife) + mann (“person, human being”, whence English man). For details on the pronunciation and spelling history, see the usage notes below. Cognate with Scots woman, weman (“woman”), Saterland Frisian Wieuwmoanske (“female person, female human, woman”).

ex: the first woman president of Spain
Cause I'm every woman / It's all in me
Listen, Holly. Thou art a good and honest man, and I fain would spare thee; but, oh! it is so hard for woman to be merciful.
I am Woman, hear me roar / In numbers too big to ignore

senses.d: A female person, usually an adult: a (generally adult) female sentient being, whether human, supernatural, elf, alien, etc.
ex: Sir, have you ever served with any Bajoran women?
To be born a woman has been to be born, within an allotted and confined space, into the keeping of men.

senses.d: A wife (or sometimes a fiancée or girlfriend).
ex: And then, when he lies with his woman, the man may concurrently be with God, and so get increase of his soul.

senses.d: A female person who is extremely fond of or devoted to a specified type of thing. (Used as the last element of a compound.)

ex: By her woman I sent your message.
Apparently the Sixty-ninth Street office of Bagby Answers, Inc., was being womaned for the day from other offices.
I have felt so many quirks of joy and grief / That the first face of neither on the start / Can woman me unto't.

senses.d: To furnish with, or unite to, a woman.
ex: And think it no addition, nor my wish, / To have him see me woman'd.

senses.d: To call (a person) “woman” in a disrespectful fashion.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French femme, from Old French fame, feme, fenme, femme, from Latin femina; ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁-m̥h₁n-éh₂ (“(the one) nursing, breastfeeding”), derivation of the verbal root *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck, suckle”).

chain.g: lady, mistress of an estate or household

ety.text: From Late Latin domna, shortened variant of Latin domina (“lady, mistress of an estate or household”), from dominus (“master”), from domus (“home”). Doublet of dama. Cognate with Sicilian donna.
Inherited from Old Spanish mugier, from Latin mulierem. Compare Portuguese mulher.

From Old Galician-Portuguese muller, moller (hence also Galician muller), from Latin mulierem (“woman; wife”), of uncertain origin. Maybe from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ- (milk; to milk). Cognate with Mirandese mulhier, Spanish mujer, Catalan muller, Italian moglie, and Romanian muiere.

ety.text: From Middle English wombe, wambe, from Old English womb, wamb (“belly, stomach; bowels; heart; womb; hollow”), from Proto-West Germanic *wambu, from Proto-Germanic *wambō (“belly, stomach, abdomen”). senses.d: In female mammals, the organ in which the young are conceived and grow until birth; the uterus.
ex: I danced myself right out the womb / Is it strange to dance so soon?
And his hede, hym semed,was enamyled with asure, and his shuldyrs shone as the golde, and his wombe was lyke mayles of a merveylous hew[…].

senses.d: The stomach of a person or creature.
A place where something is made or formed.
ex: The womb of earth the genial seed receives.
The shadows of the future hours rose dark and menacing from the womb of time [...]

senses.d: Any cavity containing and enveloping anything.
ex:
The centre spike of gold
 Which burns deep in the blue-bell's womb.

senses.d: To enclose in a womb, or as if in a womb; to breed or hold in secret.
